source.title: Statistical Vignettes on the Grokking Phenomenon

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analytically studies delayed generalization in a different, synthetic planted-feature model and validates the predicted dynamics experimentally. It is a conceptual test of grokking-like delays and their dependence on training conditions, not a reproduction on algorithmic datasets.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results concern a bilinear model on synthetic binary data with a planted predictive feature and Gaussian nuisance features. The modular-addition, mechanistic-interpretability, and other related-work findings are citations, not results from this study. The model starts with the core feature present, so it does not test discovery of an algorithmic circuit.
record.test_reason: The paper's own theorems and simulations show delayed test-target attainment after early training fitting. The setting is a planted-feature bilinear model on synthetic Gaussian data, studied under gradient flow and vanilla GD. It bears on V2 (core vs nuisance timing), V3 (non-algorithmic setting; initialization and weight decay effects), V5 (role of weight decay) and V7 (delay without optimizer or softmax artifacts). It is not an algorithmic or LLM study.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude their tractable model separates early nuisance fitting, slow core learning and test-target attainment, and gives sharp conditions and analytic plateau lengths. Weight decay is not necessary for grokking: it changes the delay and can prevent a target, but 'does not dictate whether grokking occurs'. The interpolation edge adds a further delay via a vanishing spectral gap. They suggest, without testing, that lazy-to-rich accounts reflect a similar separation of time scales.
record.recipe_differences: The original studies concern small algorithmic tasks and modular arithmetic; this paper uses a synthetic binary classification distribution with a planted core signal and Gaussian nuisance features, a bilinear student model, squared loss, and gradient flow with a gradient-descent comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on signal strength, effective weight decay, aspect ratio and proximity to interpolation, core initialization, and—in the reported comparison—gradient flow versus rescaled vanilla gradient descent.

fits_no_version.finding: Below interpolation the plateau length scales as 1/(1−γ), growing as n approaches d. In the sample-poor regime d>n, dynamics converge to a saddle with 50% test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In solvable linear or bilinear models, a critical sample size (n=d interpolation threshold), not weight-decay efficiency, sets whether and how late generalization occurs.

record.problems: The evidence is for a stylized synthetic task in which the predictive core is already present, not a network discovering an algorithm on realistic data. Experimental values are largely presented in plots without stated error bars or repeated-run uncertainty; the theoretical results are asymptotic. The Figure 10 description of regularization is garbled.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing condition was omitted from the main reported results. Extended plots in Appendix C repeat or extend the same qualitative trends; Figure 10's regularization value is not recoverable from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Entire version: no algorithmic datasets. A delay-vs-sample-size dependence exists only via aspect ratio in a synthetic model.
No circuit formation (the core feature is planted, not discovered), no Fourier algorithm, no mechanistic progress measures on real networks.
No images, text or molecules. No actual lazy-to-rich transition test; the paper only suggests an analogy. No weight-norm or initialization-scale switch in the Omnigrok sense.
No circuit-efficiency comparison, no critical dataset size derived from weight decay, no ungrokking.
No adaptive optimizers (Adam), no softmax or floating-point controls; squared loss throughout.

missing.what: Interpolation-edge runs with weight decay λ∈{1e-5,1e-4} in which b>1/zp=0.60 and the test target is not reached. Figure 1's caption also notes decay prevents grokking at very small signal.
Sample-poor regime d>n: dynamics converge to a non-generalizing saddle at 50% test accuracy (qualitative, no experiment).
Phase portraits of ‖w‖ vs θ showing fast relaxation to the slow manifold, then slow core evolution. Moderate signal shortens hitting time.

record.verdict_notes: All evidence comes from a stylized model with a planted core feature, asymptotic theorems, and single-run plots without error bars. Labels are therefore confined to this setting. 'Test accuracy' here is Φ(θ/‖w‖), a smooth function, so 'jumps' appear only on log-time axes. The V5 challenge rests on the model's parameterization, in which decay penalizes the core directly. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not use small algorithmic datasets or test whether shrinking the training set increases the delay.

Tests gradual learning of a planted core coefficient and its relation to test accuracy, but not Fourier circuits, modular addition, mechanistic circuit identification, or continuous interpretability measures of an algorithm.

Tests grokking-like delays in a synthetic non-algorithmic task and varies core initialization and weight decay. It does not test images, text, molecules, or an actual lazy-to-rich transition controlled by initialization scale or weight norm.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning, or realistic large-model data, is studied.

Tests how weight decay changes delayed test-target attainment in this model. It does not test whether weight decay selects a more efficient circuit over memorization or predict a critical dataset size.
No comparison of identifiable algorithms learned across runs, architectures, or hyperparameters.
Compares gradient flow with vanilla gradient descent and reports that the trajectories agree closely. Does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limits in softmax.

relationships.condition: Interpolation edge (γ=1), weak effective regularization (b<1/zp), synthetic planted-core model
relationships.reason: Core reaches fixed levels on scale ℓn, but the test target needs an extra 0.5ℓn log(1/ρn) while nuisance contributions shrink (R6, R7, R15–R17).
relationships.display_finding: The core reaches fixed levels on timescale ℓn, while reaching the test target requires an additional 0.5ℓn log(1/ρn) as nuisance contributions shrink.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Interpolation edge (γ=1), weak effective regularization (b<1/zp), synthetic planted-core model
source_check.reason: R6–R7 establish gradual core learning before test-target attainment, with an additional logarithmic delay while nuisance interference diminishes; R15–R17 illustrate this separation.

relationships.condition: Below interpolation (γ<1), and at the edge with strong regularization
relationships.reason: Below interpolation, nuisance weights track the core and test accuracy follows the core on the same scale (R3, R4). At the edge with b>1/zp, the core goes to 1 but generalization never comes, so core progress does not anticipate it (R8).
relationships.display_finding: Below interpolation, nuisance weights and test accuracy tracked the core on the same scale; at the edge with b>1/zp, the core reached 1 without generalization.

source_check.condition: Below interpolation (γ<1), and at the edge with strong regularization
source_check.reason: R3–R4 place core learning and test performance on the same slow scale below interpolation; R8 shows that core convergence alone is insufficient for attaining the test target.

relationships.condition: Synthetic Gaussian planted-feature data, gradient flow and vanilla GD
relationships.reason: Delayed test-target attainment after early training fit occurs on non-algorithmic data (R1, R2, R4, R7, R9, R12–R17). Delay length scales with log(1/θ0) (R18, R22–R24), and weight decay can switch attainment off (R5, R11).
relationships.display_finding: Test targets were attained after early training fit with delays scaling as log(1/θ0), while weight decay could prevent attainment.

source_check.condition: Synthetic Gaussian planted-feature data, gradient flow and vanilla GD
source_check.reason: The non-algorithmic synthetic setting exhibits delayed generalization, initialization-dependent plateau lengths and regularization-dependent attainment; it does not establish a neural lazy-to-rich transition.

relationships.condition: Same synthetic model; dependence on data properties
relationships.reason: Plateau length scales as 1/[2(1−γ)ε], set by data signal amplitude and sample-to-dimension ratio, not only the training regime. Initialization changes the delay's length but does not switch it off (R4, R18).
relationships.display_finding: Plateau length scaled as 1/[2(1−γ)ε], depending on signal amplitude and sample-to-dimension ratio; initialization altered the delay's duration without removing it.

source_check.condition: Same synthetic model; dependence on data properties
source_check.reason: R4 and equation (20) explicitly make the delay depend on signal amplitude and sample-to-dimension ratio, qualifying the claim that the training regime alone sets it.

relationships.condition: Synthetic bilinear model, where L2 decay on u,v acts as an L1 penalty on the core
relationships.reason: Delay and target attainment occur with zero decay (R9, R15–R17). Larger effective decay lengthens the plateau and above threshold prevents generalization (R5, R8, R11), the reverse of decay favouring the generalizing solution.
relationships.display_finding: Delayed target attainment occurred without decay, while larger effective decay lengthened the plateau and prevented generalization above a threshold.

relationships.reason: The delay arises under exact gradient flow and persists under discrete GD with close agreement (R9, R15, R19–R22). It does not depend on adaptive-optimizer or softmax numerics here; Adam and softmax themselves are untested.
relationships.display_finding: Delayed generalization arose under exact gradient flow and closely matching discrete gradient descent, without requiring adaptive optimization or softmax numerics.
